focus: pre-existing transatlantic reference supply, nursery mediation, collection-state scarcity and long-latency workshop stock
core_result: The 1892 expedition did not inaugurate access to American botanical material. By 1889-1891 Harvard and Hosterwitz already operated a transatlantic reference-supply ecology using plants, seeds, books, paid cultivation, circulating lists, nursery catalogues and living shipments. The journey supplemented that system by obtaining reference states and forms poorly available through remote supply. Returned expedition material then persisted as workshop stock whose activation depended on taxonomy, redundancy, biological adequacy, difficulty and production capacity.

events.mechanism: Harvard pays reasonable care expenses for American plants at Hosterwitz and, through George Lincoln Goodale, provides plants, seeds and books needed for the collection.
events.research_value: Makes transatlantic American-reference supply and local cultivation contractual infrastructure before the 1892 expedition.
guards: OCR renders the weekly garden allowance unclearly, approximately 'seven banks'; do not normalize currency without image verification.

events.mechanism: The workshop refers to a selection among American plants from a list recently sent to Goodale and asks for wild plants spanning as many new families as possible.
events.research_value: Shows that Harvard collection need was already being externalized into a portable pre-expedition selection list.
guards: Do not identify this list with the undated Corning Plant Desiderata document until the latter is inspected.

events.taxon: Fritillaria recurva as written in the letter
events.mechanism: A California bulb was sent to Hosterwitz in 1890, flowered there, differed in colour from published descriptions, but was judged sufficiently characteristic for modelling; Goodale was expected to identify the resulting model.
events.research_value: Remote supply could solve material access while leaving taxonomic closure unresolved.
guards: Do not crosswalk automatically to the annotated shipment-list entry Fritillaria parviflora, Torr.

events.evidence: Rudolf looked forward to collecting American forms 'hitherto inaccessible to us'.
events.calibration: Because American plants were already reaching Hosterwitz through the 1889-1891 supply system, 'inaccessible' should refer to residual forms, states or observations, not to American flora as a whole.

events.mechanism: Rudolf planned to visit Mr. Gillett in Southwick, identifying him as the supplier of catalogues and Cypripedium material, to discuss future acquisition of seeds and plants.
events.associated_observation: Rudolf said the current journey yielded little seed because plants were generally in spring condition and seeds usually began later, around July.
events.research_value: Field travel was expected to reconnect with and extend the remote nursery supply network.
events.guard: The present corpus does not yet prove the proposed 1892 Southwick visit occurred.

events.mechanism: Rudolf and Blankinship visited the Southwick nursery; Rudolf obtained three or four plants and then collected during the walk back toward Westfield.
events.research_value: Demonstrates later physical integration of nursery and field acquisition.
events.chronology_guard: Do not use this documented 1895 visit as evidence that the proposed 1892 visit took place.

events.evidence: Rudolf said material remaining from the first journey should cover only two more shipments and that several very complicated first-journey subjects had been postponed for lack of time and were still waiting.
events.research_value: The 1892 return became finite heterogeneous stock; difficult references could remain dormant behind later production.

events.evidence: Rudolf recalled that early consignments could be filled with easy/easier subjects from abundant material, but the 'fillers got scarce' as the collection developed; fixed annual expectations of first 120 and later 100 models became increasingly hard.
events.research_value: Collection saturation changed the marginal difficulty of useful additions; scarcity was representational as well as botanical.

events.evidence: Rudolf counted about eighty pieces/species of 'secured material yet to be done' and reported Goodale/Greenman determination work on poorly determined California-journey plants.
events.research_value: Some journey-derived reference stock remained operationally and taxonomically active about a decade later.
events.guard: Image-check quantitative and taxonomic wording before publication quotation.

events.evidence: Rudolf says he uses an American plant obtained locally when it is a valuable 'gap-filler' not represented in the collection, while some journey material represents types already present; he also says he still has about eighty species of journey material at hand.
events.research_value: Directly separates physical availability, journey provenance, collection redundancy and production usefulness.
events.guard: Do not assign this text to the dated 24 February 1902 letter until source alignment is completed.

access_regimes.institutional_compression: Botanical gardens concentrate cultivated access, specialists and work space.
access_regimes.ecological_extension: Wild excursions extend the reference set and habitat encounter beyond institutional collections.

gate_B_revision.principle: Journey provenance did not confer automatic production priority. A reference could remain secured stock for years while taxonomy, redundancy, condition and workshop capacity changed around it.

working_claims: Remote supply and fieldwork were complementary access regimes, not serial replacements.
Inaccessibility was relative to the biological and epistemic state required for modelling, not to geography alone.
The collection itself generated scarcity as easy non-redundant fillers disappeared.
The expedition returned as stock whose members could remain inactive for years before staged reactivation.
A growing collection changes the cost structure of the next useful model.
The 1892 journey was a mobile intervention inside an already distributed supply ecology.
